drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Look at what's guarding your bishop on d4 — only the queen, along the f6-e5-d4 diagonal. Qe6 offers a trade right into Qxe6 Rxe6, and the second your queen leaves f6 that diagonal is empty, so Rxd4 just wins the bishop clean. The position was roughly balanced before this, and now you're down a full piece for nothing. c5 keeps the tension instead: after Bd5 cxb4 axb4 Rxa2 Bxa2 you actually win the exchange on a2, all while your queen stays on f6 babysitting d4. Before you trade queens, always ask what stops being defended once she's gone.

drills.explanation: h5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Bb5 ran into Qxg4+, costing about 3.9 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g4 is just hanging, and because your king sits on the g-file, Qxg4+ comes with check — Bb5 grabs at the rook on f1 but completely ignores that. After Qxg4+ Kf8 Qh5 you're down a piece and your king's stuck in the corner while the queen keeps finding new threats. You were only slightly worse to begin with (0.9), and this turns it into a rout. h5 was the fix: it hands the h6 pawn a job of guarding g4, so if White ever grabs the knight you just recapture, and only then do you get to swing your pieces around. Secure your loose piece before you throw the next punch.

drills.explanation: Qb5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, g6 ran into Qc4+, costing about 4.8 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Racheeeedgr (827) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: g6 blocks your own king's escape square on g7 and leaves permanent holes on f6 and h6 right as White's queen sits actively on e4 hunting checks. Qc4+ forces Kh7 — the only square left — and then g4 hits your queen with tempo, and by the time it settles your winning endgame has evaporated. You were clearly winning at -2.8 despite being down pawns, purely because your queen was so active and White's king so exposed; g6 throws that away for nothing. Qb5 keeps the queen prowling and lets your king walk safely through the center instead (...Kf8, ...Kf2). In queen endings, don't loosen pawns near your own king to 'feel safe' — it's usually the opposite.

drills.title: vs Racheeeedgr (827) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: The knight jumps to e4 with nothing covering that square, and Qf5+ punishes it immediately — check first, dragging your king to h8, then Qxe4 just scoops the knight for free. You were already under some pressure here (1.8) despite the extra piece, and Ne4 hands the material edge right back. Qe8 keeps the queen central and connected, ready to trade checks after Qc2+ Kh8 Qc4 Qe1 Qc8+ without ever leaving anything on an undefended square. In a queen ending, every time you move a piece, ask first whether the queen can just take it with check.

drills.title: vs AliceAylin (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Kf3 doesn't actually do anything for you, and worse, you have to walk straight back with Ke2 next move anyway — that's a free tempo you're handing Black, and he uses it to grab the b4 pawn outright with Rxb4. You were already a touch worse here (-0.7) and this just bleeds more of the position for nothing. Nf3 instead keeps the knight useful, rerouting toward d4 to centralize and set up g5/fxg5 counterplay — b4 may still fall eventually in that line too, but you're getting real activity for it instead of losing a move and a pawn together. Before you move your king, check whether it's actually improving something or just marking time.

drills.title: vs AliceAylin (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your rook on c2 was the only thing guarding the c3 pawn, and Rd2 pulls it off that square — Black just takes with Rxc3, completely free. Ne4 hits the rook with tempo but you never get the pawn back, you just chase it to a3 before settling with Rc2, and your comfortable 1.6 edge turns into something close to equal or worse. Kd3 keeps the king right there defending c3 while staying active — Bxa6 Ra2 and then Rxa7 nets you real material on the other wing instead. Before you move a piece off a square, always check what it was holding together.

drills.explanation: Nh5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Rh8 ran into Bxf7#, costing about 23.6 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs NguyenTuanHai555 (860) — Vienna Game Anderssen Defense
drills.coachNote: This is the big one: your king had already marched up to g6, and White's bishop on c4, knight on g5, and queen on h4 are all pointed straight at it. Rh8 does nothing about that, and Bxf7 is mate on the spot — the bishop checks from f7, you can't take it because the knight on g5 guards that square, and every flight square is either covered by the queen down the h-file or blocked by your own pieces. You were completely winning at +3.6 and it ends in an instant mate. Nh5 was the fix — it hits the queen on h4 directly and forces trades that dismantle the mating pieces before your king is ever checked. Whenever your king's come forward, scan every check the opponent has before you play anything else.

drills.title: vs NguyenTuanHai555 (860) — Vienna Game Anderssen Defense
drills.coachNote: Bg4 pokes at the queen on f3, but White just steps to g3 — and that's actually a better square for her, since your own h6 push already gave her a hook and now she eyes the light squares toward your king while your knight on b8 is still sitting home undeveloped. You were already a bit worse here (1.3), and this spends a tempo attacking a piece that simply sidesteps for free. Nc6 develops your last minor piece and keeps things flexible, and after Qg3 you can hit the queen again with Nh5, keeping the initiative instead of handing White an improving move. Don't spend a move attacking a piece that can just step aside — develop first.

drills.title: vs liwanag22 (867) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You were already down big here, and your king on e2 has zero luft — that's the real danger. Rh1 attacks the queen on h2, but Black just plays Qxf2#: check, and every flight square is covered — d3 and f3 by the pawn on e4, e1, e3 and f1 simply because they sit next to the queen on f2. Neither knight on c2 nor d2 can jump in to stop it, so it's mate on the spot. The move that kept you fighting was Rxg3, ripping away the pawn propping up her queen on h2 — after Bd6 Nf1 Qh5+ Kd2 you're worse, but alive.

drills.title: vs liwanag22 (867) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's queen has invaded to g2, and Rg1 looks like it hits her, but the moment your rook leaves h1 your pawn on h3 loses its only defender — Black just plays Qxh3, dodging the attack and grabbing a pawn for free, then even lands a check with Nbd2 Ne7 Qa4+. Rh2 does the same job of attacking the queen but without that flaw: the rook still guards h3 from h2, so she has no safe square and has to trade, Qxh2 Nxh2, leaving you the exchange up. When you attack a piece, always check what square you're vacating and what it was protecting.

drills.coachNote: Black's king is stuck on e7 in the middle of the board — that's your real edge, not a queen trade. Qg5+ looks natural but Black just plays Qxg5, Nxg5, and the queens vanish along with your attacking chances against that king. Qf4 keeps them on: after Qd6 Qg5+ Qf6 Qxd5 you still scoop up the pawn on d5, but this time with queens still on and Black's king still exposed, so your winning chances stay alive instead of shrinking into a bare endgame. When the enemy king is stuck in the center, don't offer the trade that lets it hide.

drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: Black's king is still on e7, uncastled and sitting in the open — that's the whole story, and it means you should be hunting checks, not pawns. Nxh7 grabs material, but it lets Black play Rd8 and Qf6+ Ke8, and suddenly the position calms down and you even give a pawn back with gxf4. Nd5+ was the shot: your other knight jumps in with check, and after exd5 Rfe1+ Kd6 Qxf8+ you're winning the rook on f8 with check while the king gets dragged even further from safety. With a king still in the center, always look for the check before the snack.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king on e2 has nowhere to run — that's what you needed to see before reaching for the pawn on e5. Qxe5+ is check, but it lets White block with Ne4, and after Bxe4 Qc1 O-O-O the king slips to safety and you're left merely winning instead of finishing the game right there. Nf4+ was the killer blow: it's check, the king is forced to e3 with no other square, and then Bc5# — your bishop from d5 delivers mate. When a king is this boxed in, scan for the check that leaves zero escape squares before you play the one that just wins a pawn.

Qg3+ keeps the king running instead: it's forced to e2, then Qxe5+ grabs the pawn on e5 with check again, and after Kf2 Qd4+ Ke2 you're still generating threats while White never gets a free tempo to consolidate. When you've got a king this exposed, keep firing checks — every quiet move you play instead is a free move for them to defend.

drills.coachNote: Your knight jump to g4 lands on a completely undefended square — h6 only guards g5, not g4 — so White's queen on d1 simply glides down the open d1-g4 diagonal and plays Qxg4, and you've dropped a full piece for nothing. That's the cost of jumping in before checking who's watching the landing square. The right move was e5 first, striking White's d4 pawn; only after dxe5 does Ng4 actually work, because now the knight lands with a real target and forces Nf3 in response. drills.coachNote: Your king on g8 has thin cover — h6's pushed, g7 is the only real guard, and White's bishop on f5 is eyeing e6. Playing d4 ignores that: White hits with Be6+, and after Kh8 the queen swings to g6 threatening mate on g7, with Be4 finishing the job — a position where you were already better turns into a mating attack on your own king. Qg5 handles it instead: it meets Be6+ calmly with Kh8, and after f4 you get Qg3+, hitting White's own king still stuck on e1. Principle: when your king's cover is thin, answer the checks before pushing pawns.

Grabbing the bishop with Re3 ignores that: White hits Bd5+, and after Kf8 comes Rc8+, forcing Re8 and letting White's rook and bishop start harassing your king with checks — exactly how a dead-won position gets shaky. Rf8 was the simple answer: it tucks the rook back to guard the back rank and keep the king safe, and after Rxa7, Rxf6 you're still completely winning, just without giving White anything to grab onto. Principle: when your king has no pawn cover, protect it before grabbing extra material, especially when you're already winning big.

Your own rook on e8 would normally back that square up too, but it's blocked by your bishop on e7, so it's really two attackers against one defender. White plays Nxe4, you recapture Nxe4, and Rxe4 just wins the piece back — you're down a full piece for nothing. Be6 was the safe square instead, guarded by f7, and after Bxe6, fxe6 the position stays roughly balanced. Rd7 was the move: it drops onto the seventh rank immediately, and when Black tries Rd6 to challenge it, Bxd6 just wins the rook outright since your bishop on e5 already covers d6. drills.title: vs Twister21checkersChess (676) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You're up a queen and bishop for a rook, so this should be a formality, but g4 ignores the one real danger on the board: black's pawns on a3 and c3 are two steps from queening, with the rook on d8 ready to escort them via checks. Sure enough, Rd1+ forces your king to g2, and Rd5 activates the rook before you finally play Rxc3 - four moves late, dropping your edge from +13.8 to +9.4. Playing Rxc3 immediately erases the danger outright, and after Kh7 Ke2 e5 Rc7 you march the king up and mop up cleanly. When you're crushing, spend the move killing the opponent's one dangerous resource, not on autopilot.

drills.title: vs Sir_Rah_123 (819) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: The real feature here is the pawn on b7 - it's one move from capturing your rook on a8 and queening, and that rook is lost no matter what you play. The question is just where your king stands when it happens. Qd7 leaves the king on e8, so bxa8=Q+ comes with check, forcing Ke7 and then Bg5+ Kf7 - your king gets dragged into the open while you're still untangling, and the eval swings over 13 points. Kf7 accepts the same loss on a8 but gets the king off the back rank first, so bxa8=Q Rxa8 happens without check and you stay coordinated. When something bad is forced, tuck your king away before you let it happen, not after.

You have to retreat with Bc8, undoing the development you just did, and after dxc6 bxc6 you're left with doubled c-pawns and a bishop back on its start square - a real structural loss for nothing. Be7 sidesteps the whole idea because it isn't on a square d5 can hit, so when white does play d5 you just reroute the knight with Nb8-d7, a completely normal regrouping plan. Before you park a piece somewhere, check whether a pawn push can hit it together with something that's already there.

Before you send a piece to grab a pawn, check what square a knight jump can land on next.

Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: At -0.6 you had the more pleasant position, with your knight sitting deep on c4 and White's queenside pawns stretched out to b4 and b5. Castling is a safe habit, but it ignored the moment: a6 strikes right at the base of that pawn chain, and after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook swings to a wonderfully active square, keeping White on the back foot. Instead O-O let White play the calm Qe2, tuck the king in, and start untangling — your edge quietly evaporates because you gave up a full tempo when there was a real target to hit. When your opponent's pawns are overextended, strike them before you castle, not after.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Ng4 just hangs the knight — White's queen sits on d1, and the diagonal d1-e2-f3-g4 is completely open, so Qxg4 wins the piece with no trick needed at all. You pushed e5 for some activity afterward, but a knight down is a knight down — you went from a roughly balanced -0.2 to a lost position, and only your opponent's rating saved you this time. c5 was the calm, correct idea: it grabs queenside space and prepares Nc6, and after Re1 Nc6 b4 b6 you're simply developing into a healthy structure instead of gambling a piece. Before jumping a knight into enemy territory, always check which diagonals the opponent's queen already covers.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: You were already crushing at -4.3, but Rad8 overlooks that your bishop on e6 needed attention — White's dark-squared bishop swings to h6, and once you're forced to answer with g6, Bxe6 simply wins that bishop, since fxe6 is forced and your huge edge shrinks. Sharper was Bxa2: your bishop already sits on the a2-e6 diagonal and that pawn is undefended, so you just grab it for free, and after Rxa2 Rae8 you keep the initiative rolling instead of handing White a way to trade off your good bishop. When you're this far ahead, look for the free material your pieces already attack before playing a quiet developing move.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You were winning big at +4.8, and the position was screaming for Nxc6 — your knight on e5 forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8 at once. After Qd6 you simply take Nxd8, and following Qxd8 you grab another pawn with Qxg5, putting the game away. Instead you played the slow a4, and that one tempo let Black strike first with Nxe5, seizing the initiative right in the center where your knights had been doing the work. From there the position turned, and a completely winning game slipped away. When you've got two pieces eyeing forks like that, cash in immediately — a prophylactic pawn move can hand the initiative straight to your opponent.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your b4 pawn was the only guard on your knight sitting on c5. Pushing it to b5 pulls that guard away and gifts Black's knight on c6 a free shot — instead of running, it just grabs your knight on e5. You snatch a pawn back with bxa6, but after bxa6 your remaining knight on c5 has nowhere to go but the ugly square b3, and you've dropped a full piece — +1.2 to losing, just like that. Nxc6 was sitting right there: take the piece under fire before it takes yours. After bxc6 Qd3 Nxc5 bxc5 a5 you trade down cleanly and keep your material intact.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Your rook already owns the 7th rank and your bishop on f6 has Black's king boxed in — Rxf7 is mate in a few moves: after Re2, Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8# with the bishop sealing every escape square. Instead Qg5 sends your queen off duty, and Black's queen and rook on b2/c2 pounce on your weakened kingside: Rxf2 grabs a pawn, and after Qe5, Rf3, Rf1 it's your own king on g1 getting mated. You went from completely won (+20) to lost. When a forced mate is sitting on the board, play the most forcing move available — don't wander off with a 'nice-looking' queen move while your own king's defenses are unguarded.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Your queen on c4 is already staring straight down the c-file at Black's rook on c8 — nothing defends it. Qxc8 just wins the rook for free. Instead you played Qd5, taking your queen off that file and letting the rook escape, and Black's queen on b2 goes to work instead, snapping up Qxa3 and then Qxh3 while your own attack stalls. That's how a completely winning position (+19.9) bleeds pawns and initiative. Qxc8 was the simple, correct move — after Qxc8 Qb5 Re8 Qf1+ Rxf1 you trade down into a trivially won endgame. Before shifting your queen to a 'better' square, check whether it's already winning something concrete right where it stands.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: This is the exact same shape biting you again two moves after the last one — your bishop on f4 is hanging to the pawn on g5, and Bf5+ with the other bishop doesn't fix that. Black just plays e6, your bishop trudges back to c2, and gxf4 quietly mops up the piece you left behind. This time there's no need for sacrifices either — Nxg5 simply wins the loose pawn clean: after fxg5 Bxg5 you're up material with an active bishop, and Nf6 Qf3 keeps pressing the king still stuck on d7. Before playing a check just because it's available, scan the board first for a piece that's simply hanging and take it.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look past the check — your bishop on f4 is already hanging to the pawn on g5, and moving your OTHER bishop doesn't change that. Bf5+ just burns a move: Black blocks with e6, your bishop retreats to c2, and only then does gxf4 quietly collect the real prize — you lose a bishop for nothing. The engine's e4 accepts that f4 is falling anyway, but cashes it in for value: after e4 gxf4 exd5, the center rips open, your pawn hits the knight on c6, and Qa4+ grabs more tempo. Same material loss, totally different compensation — if a piece is going to fall, make sure you're getting paid for it.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps e4-g5 to hit White's knight on f3, but g5 is covered — White's bishop on c1 sits on the c1-h6 diagonal, and Bxg5 just wins your knight outright. You get f6 in to poke the bishop, but Nxe5 grabs your loose e5 pawn on the way too, so you're down a full piece for nothing — equal flips to lost. That e5 pawn was undefended regardless of what you played; Nd6 was the safe answer, tucking the knight home first. After Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 Bg6 Bf4 you're only down that one pawn, not a piece. Before jumping a piece in to 'attack' a square, check who else is watching it.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: You dodged a bullet last move when your opponent grabbed the e5 pawn instead of your hanging knight — but that knight is STILL sitting on g5, and Bc1 is still aiming right at it. Playing Be7 develops a piece but ignores the real problem: Bxg5 wins the knight, and because your bishop just landed on e7, it doesn't even survive — Bxe7 Qxe7 trades it off too, and you're down a full piece with nothing to show for it. Ne6 was the move: rescue the piece under fire before you develop anything else. A hanging piece always outranks a developing move, no matter how natural the developing move looks.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's queen on d8 was a real target — Bc7 hits it directly and forces a response on your terms: after Bc7 Qd7 b6 Nc6 Ra4 f6, you clamp down with real space and keep the initiative. Instead e4 looks natural but gives Black a free tempo to defuse the whole idea with Bd7, so the queen gets support before you can harass it, and your edge shrinks from +0.8 to worse than equal. You still won the game, but the lesson holds: scan for the forcing shot that makes your opponent react before reaching for the quiet, natural-looking move.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your b5 pawn is hanging and Qc3 does nothing to protect it — Black plays Bd7, heading right at it, and after Qc5 Bxb5 you've dropped a clean pawn while Black's rooks swing into action with Rfb1 barely making up for it. The move was Qc5, hitting the queen on b6 directly: Black has to retreat to d8, then Bd6 skewers the rook on f8, forcing Re8, and Bxe7 just wins the knight outright since nothing's left guarding it. Same lesson both times — ask what your queen move actually attacks or defends, not just where it looks safe.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, up more than four pawns, and Nf5+ was sitting right there — a check that forks the king on g3 and the rook on g7 at once. Play it and after Kf4 Nxg7 you just win the rook clean and the game's basically over. Instead Nb7 sends your knight to an undefended square, and White answers Rc7+, forcing Kd8, then Rxb7 scoops the knight for nothing — your whole winning position is gone in two moves. When you're this far ahead, scan for checks and forks first; they often end the game outright.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were up more than six pawns, completely winning, and there was a free shot on the board: Bxg3+ grabs a pawn with check, forces Kxg3, and only then do you trade rooks with Rxd1 — you come out an exchange and a pawn ahead with an easy win. Instead Rd7 just parks your rook on a square your knight on c6 doesn't actually defend, so Rxd7 wins your rook for nothing, and White keeps grabbing more with bxc6 right after. Before trading rooks down a file, check for a forcing in-between move first — free material like that doesn't wait around.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your knight on e6 has the black king on e7 completely boxed in — it covers d8 and f8, so Qxb7+, taking the pawn while checking along the seventh rank, leaves Black nothing better than blocking with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate. Instead exd4 just grabs a central pawn and lets that mating shot slip away; the game continues with Bg7, dxc5, Qc7, Rd7+ and you're still winning big, but you traded a forced mate for a long grind. When the enemy king is this stuck, look past the obvious capture and ask if there's a check that ends it outright.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same king on e7, still boxed in, and you had Rd7+ — sac the rook with check, and after the forced Qxd7 your knight on e6 recaptures with Nxd7, winning Black's queen for a rook. That swap alone puts the game away for good. Instead Nd7 just repositions the knight without cashing in, and after Bg7 Black's king slips out of danger while you're only shuffling with Rd6 and Rad1 — still winning, but you gave back a big chunk of your edge. When a piece like your knight on e6 is dominating squares around the enemy king, look for the forcing shot before quietly repositioning it.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your queen heads to h4, and nothing defends that square — Black's queen on e7 has a clear diagonal straight to it and just plays Qxh4, and you've handed away your queen for free in a position you were already losing. That's the whole story: no piece watches h4, so the moment Black's queen has that diagonal open, it's simply gone. Qa3 keeps the queen safe and active where Black can't touch it, and you keep fighting on with moves like Re8 and c4 — down material, but still in the game. Before sending your queen off alone, check every line running into that square, especially diagonals.
